mean/answer: An embedding table turns tokens into vectors, so that a model can compute with text. But in the end, it has to answer in tokens.
mean/pick: Say it has read cats chase, and must write the next word. It has to pick one token from its vocabulary: here just four, cats, chase, mice and dogs.
mean/h: Whatever it has worked out about that next word sits in one vector, h, with d numbers, just like an embedding. Here d is two, so h is an arrow: two, one.
mean/rows: Now give every token an arrow of its own, too: a row of d weights for each token.
mean/agree: Which token does h mean? The one whose arrow points most the way h does. The dot product measures exactly that: positive when two arrows agree, zero at a right angle, negative when they point apart.
mean/mice: Mice's row is three, one, close to h. Three times two, plus one times one, makes seven.
mean/rest: Dogs scores two. Cats, at a right angle, scores zero, and chase, pointing away, minus three.
mean/win: The highest score wins, so the model writes mice. It is the linear classifier again, with one class for every token.
matrix/stack: To score every token at once, stack the rows into one matrix, W U: one row per token, and one column per number in h.
matrix/name: The U is for unembedding. The embedding table turned a token into a vector, and this matrix turns a vector back into tokens.
matrix/shape: Its shape is V by d, with V for the size of the vocabulary: here, four by two.
matrix/all: W U times h dots every row with h at once. Out comes s, one score per token: zero, minus three, seven and two.
matrix/logits: Raw scores like these, of any size and either sign, are often called logits. The highest still wins: mice, at seven.
matrix/argmax: Picking the top score this way has a name: the argmax. It is not the score itself, seven, but where it sits: position two, which is mice.
matrix/many: A model often has a vector like h at every position in the text. Stack three of them, three by d, and each row is scored on its own: three by V, a row of scores per position.
tie/compare: Now set W U beside the embedding table, E. Both have a row for every token, with d numbers in each: the same shape, V by d.
tie/same: And they hold the same tokens. The words a model reads and the words it writes come from one vocabulary.
tie/papers: So in 2017, two papers used one matrix for both jobs: one by Ofir Press and Lior Wolf, and one by Hakan Inan and his colleagues.
tie/tied: Tie them, and W U is E. Each token is scored with its own row of E: its own embedding.
tie/Ej: Write E j for row j of E, the embedding of token j.
tie/sj: Then token j's score, s j, is E j dotted with h. It is high when h points the way that token's embedding does.
tie/better: Both papers found that tied models predicted text better than untied ones, with far fewer numbers to learn.
tie/both: Untied, the two matrices hold two times V times d learned numbers. With fifty thousand tokens and d of seven hundred sixty-eight, that is seventy-six point eight million.
tie/save: Tied, they are one V by d table, so tying saves half: thirty-eight point four million.
